title: The Awakening
author: Kate Chopin
openingText: A green and yellow parrot, which hung in a cage outside the door, kept repeating over and over: "Allez vous-en! Allez vous-en! Sapristi!" That is all right!
about: Edna Pontellier is a married woman in 1890s New Orleans who starts to notice she is not who she was supposed to be. The novel follows her attempts to become herself. Louisiana society makes this impossible.

angleCards.title: The discovery of personhood.
angleCards.text: Edna doesn't just fall in love or rebel — she discovers she exists as a self. That awakening is a genuine philosophical event, and the tragedy is that 1890s Louisiana has no place for what she has become. I want to track how Chopin stages that discovery step by step.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow Edna's awakening as a philosophical problem — she discovers she is a person, not a role, and there is nowhere in her society for that person to go.

angleCards.title: What the ending means.
angleCards.text: The novel's final pages are among the most contested in American literature. Is it tragedy, escape, or both? I want to build toward that ending with the question open — reading for the evidence that supports each interpretation and deciding for myself.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the ending carefully — whether it is defeat or the only kind of freedom available to Edna, and what Chopin actually intends us to feel.

angleCards.title: Against the marriage plot.
angleCards.text: Austen and Brontë built worlds where a good marriage was a genuine resolution. Chopin refuses that. I want to read her refusal carefully — what she saw that they didn't, or couldn't say, and why the novel still scandalised readers in 1899.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read The Awakening against the marriage plots of Austen and Brontë — understanding what Chopin refuses to accept that they accepted, and what that refusal costs Edna.

angleCards.title: The language of the sea.
angleCards.text: Chopin returns to the sea again and again throughout the novel — as liberation, as sensuality, as danger. I want to track every appearance of water and understand how Chopin uses it to chart Edna's inner state and prepare the ending.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow what the sea means throughout the novel — Chopin keeps returning to it, and it seems to mean both freedom and dissolution at the same time.

cast.name: Edna Pontellier
cast.description: A Kentucky-born woman married into Creole society in New Orleans. The novel is entirely her interior — her growing awareness of herself as a person rather than a role, and the consequences of that awareness.

cast.name: Léonce Pontellier
cast.description: A prosperous businessman who loves Edna in the only way he knows how — as property to be proud of, a household to be maintained. He is not cruel. He simply cannot see her.

cast.name: Robert Lebrun
cast.description: A charming young man who makes a habit of devoted attentions to married women — flirtatiously, harmlessly. With Edna, something goes differently. He becomes the occasion of her awakening without quite intending to.

cast.name: Adèle Ratignolle
cast.description: Edna's closest friend — devoted, beautiful, entirely defined by her role as wife and mother. She is the life Edna is supposed to want and cannot bring herself to imitate. Her warmth is genuine; her worldview is a cage.

cast.name: Mademoiselle Reisz
cast.description: A brilliant, eccentric pianist who lives alone, answers to no one, and is disliked by almost everyone. She represents the other available life — freedom purchased at the cost of every comfort and connection.

cast.name: The Sea
cast.description: Not a character but a force — the Gulf of Mexico at Grand Isle, returning throughout the novel. It means freedom, sensuality, danger, and dissolution. Its final appearance is the novel's destination.
